characterList.description: A middle-aged man with short, graying hair, wearing a dark suit and a patterned tie. He is the Governor of the Bank of England.
characterList.name: Mark Carney

content_metadata.description: Mark Carney, Governor of the Bank of England, elaborates on the Bank's strategy to support future financial developments, highlighting digital innovation, regulatory measures, and SME funding.

qAndA.answer: He states that one-fifth of all sales in the UK were online last year, and that this is expected to increase to one-quarter next year.
qAndA.question: What specific example does Mark Carney give about the changing nature of commerce?

qAndA.answer: He refers to the funding gap experienced by SMEs. The Bank of England aims to address this through the RTGS rebuild, enabling platform-based finance for SMEs.
qAndA.question: What is the 'biggest funding gap' Mark Carney refers to, and how is the Bank of England trying to address it?

qAndA.answer: He uses the phrase 'with an open mind, but not an open door,' indicating a willingness to explore innovation while maintaining regulatory oversight.
qAndA.question: What phrase does Mark Carney use to describe the Bank of England's approach to innovations like stablecoins?

qAndA.answer: Mark Carney states that it could range between £2 billion and £4.5 billion per year.
qAndA.question: How much money is estimated to be spent annually by the financial industry on regulatory submissions?

qAndA.answer: The video repeatedly uses an animation of a blue globe, covered with lines, dots, and digital icons, to visually represent the vastness and interconnectedness of data.
qAndA.question: What visual metaphor is used throughout the video to represent data and its growing role in finance?

activities.description: Mark Carney is delivering a speech to the camera.

mood.description: Neutral, then slightly positive. Mark Carney begins with a neutral introduction, but transitions to a more hopeful tone when mentioning the future of finance.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Transition from neutral to positive when Mark talks about 'creating the future of finance'.

narrativeProgression.description: Mark Carney welcomes viewers to the Sibos conference in London.
He highlights London's historical and current role as a leading financial center and FinTech hub.
He introduces the Bank of England's ambitious plan to support the development of the future of finance.

scenes.thematicElements: The future of finance, innovation, London as a financial center, the role of the Bank of England.
scenes.title: Introduction and Setting the Stage

videoEditingDetails.description: Intro screen with the Sibos logo, 'LONDON', and dates. The background is a solid turquoise color.
Transition to a video of Mark Carney.
Lower third graphic appears with Mark Carney's name and title.
Transition to a blurred image of a building with columns. The text 'THE FUTURE OF FINANCE' appears in large letters.

mood.description: Neutral, with hints of optimism. Mark Carney outlines the challenges and opportunities of the digital economy.

narrativeProgression.description: Mark Carney explains the increasing digitization and hyper-connectivity of the world.
He acknowledges the opportunities and challenges this brings.
He emphasizes the need for a new finance to serve the digital economy, one that balances innovation with resilience.
He states this requires a new Bank of England that enables innovation, empowers competition, and ensures the resilience of the financial system.

scenes.thematicElements: Digital economy, innovation, resilience, the role of central banks.
scenes.title: The Future of Finance: A New Economy and a New Bank

videoEditingDetails.description: Text overlays appear on the blurred building image highlighting 'INCREASED - digitisation - connectivity'.
Transition to a blank turquoise screen with the text 'This new economy requires a new finance'.
A blurred image of the Bank of England logo appears, with text overlays highlighting 'Enable innovation' 'Empower competition'.

mood.description: Neutral, slightly positive when highlighting the bank's initiatives. Mark Carney explains the Bank of England's actions to enable the digital economy.

narrativeProgression.description: Mark Carney focuses on enabling the digital economy.
He notes the decline in cash usage and the increasing expectation for real-time transactions.
He explains how the Bank is leveling the playing field by giving non-banks access to the core payments system (RTGS).
He highlights the Bank's role in opening access and allowing firms to compete with banks.
He notes the increasing number of payment service providers joining RTGS.
He mentions the plans to rebuild RTGS to provide API access and standardized payment tagging.

scenes.thematicElements: Open banking, payments systems, data access, competition in financial services.
scenes.title: Enabling the Digital Economy: Open Access and Data

videoEditingDetails.description: Transition to a blurred image of a different building with columns.
Blurred image of the Bank of England logo reappears, with the text 'RTGS rebuild: to provide API access to users to read and write payments data'.
Transition to a blank turquoise screen with the text '5 payment service providers already members of RTGS'.

mood.description: Neutral, concerned when discussing the funding gap, then positive when presenting the bank's solution.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Slight shift to a more concerned tone when discussing the lack of track record for SMEs.
Transition back to a more positive tone when discussing the potential for data to help close the SME funding gap.

narrativeProgression.description: Mark Carney shifts focus to the challenge of the SME funding gap.
He explains how the RTGS rebuild can help by enabling platform-based finance for SMEs.
This can contribute to closing the biggest funding gap in the country.
He mentions that almost half of SMEs don't use external finance due to hurdles in applying from banks.
He attributes part of the problem to the intangible nature of assets many SMEs seek to borrow against.

scenes.thematicElements: SME funding gap, intangible assets, data-driven lending.
scenes.title: Addressing the SME Funding Gap

videoEditingDetails.description: 'RTGS rebuild' text changes to 'to help close the funding gap for SMEs'.
Transition to a blue globe animation covered in lines and dots. Text 'Use data to identify all information that adds value to their business' appears.
Transition back to Mark Carney.

mood.description: Neutral, cautious when discussing stablecoins, then positive when outlining the bank's approach.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Slight shift to a cautious tone when talking about the need for regulations for stablecoins.
Transition back to a more positive tone when describing the potential benefits of stablecoins.

narrativeProgression.description: Mark Carney acknowledges the potential for data-driven lending to close the SME funding gap.
He transitions to the topic of stablecoins and other payment innovations.
He explains their potential to improve financial inclusion and lower payment costs.
He emphasizes the Bank of England's approach to these innovations: 'with an open mind, but not an open door.'
He stresses the need for regulatory frameworks to ensure stability and prevent systemic risks.

scenes.thematicElements: Stablecoins, payment innovations, financial inclusion, regulatory frameworks, risk management.
scenes.title: Stablecoins: Balancing Innovation with Stability

videoEditingDetails.description: Transition to a screen with various digital icons, including a computer, smartphone, car, and house. Text 'RTGS rebuild to help close the funding gap for SMEs' remains.
Text changes to 'But this shouldn't be the case in a data-rich world.'
Transition to the blue globe animation, this time with continents and a radiating light.
Transition back to Mark Carney.
Transition to a screen with a blurred Bank of England logo and a large, stylized Bitcoin symbol. Text 'Approach innovation with an open mind, not an open door' appears.

mood.description: Neutral, authoritative. Mark Carney outlines the Bank of England's leadership role in shaping the future of finance.

narrativeProgression.description: Mark Carney summarizes the Bank of England's approach to innovation, balancing openness with careful regulation.
He highlights the Bank's leadership in international forums on financial innovation and regulation.
He transitions to the topic of data as a key competitive advantage in financial services.

scenes.thematicElements: International cooperation, data as a competitive advantage, financial regulation.
scenes.title: The Bank of England: Leading the Way

videoEditingDetails.description: Transition back to Mark Carney.
Transition to a blurred background of connected lines and dots. The text 'Data is key to competitive advantage' appears in large letters.

mood.description: Neutral, factual. Mark Carney explains the importance of data management and the bank's efforts to use data efficiently.

narrativeProgression.description: Mark Carney emphasizes the importance of data management for competitive advantage in financial services.
He highlights the adoption of cloud computing and AI in the banking sector.
He notes the significant growth in data volume and the challenges it poses for supervision.
He mentions potential savings through efficient data management.
He announces the Bank's review on hosting and using regulatory data and plans for proof-of-concept projects to explore automatic data extraction and analysis using AI and ML.

scenes.thematicElements: Data management, cloud computing, AI, regulatory data, supervisory efficiency.
scenes.title: Data Management and Supervisory Efficiency

videoEditingDetails.description: Text overlays appear on the blurred background, 'Collection' 'Storage' 'Analysis'.
Transition to the blue globe animation with digital icons and fast-moving lines and binary code. Text 'Banking 2nd biggest global spender on AI systems' appears.

mood.description: Neutral, hopeful, and collaborative. Mark Carney concludes by emphasizing the need for collaboration to shape the future of finance.

narrativeProgression.description: Mark Carney reiterates the need for efficient data management in financial regulation.
He highlights opportunities for collaboration in developing more efficient processes.
He reiterates the potential of new finance for inclusive and sustainable growth.
He emphasizes the Bank of England's commitment to enabling this future.
He calls for engagement and collaboration with innovators to achieve these goals.
He encourages viewers to learn more about the Bank's plans at the conference.
He concludes his speech with a message of hope and collaboration.

scenes.thematicElements: Collaboration, innovation, data management, sustainable growth, inclusive finance.
scenes.title: Collaboration and the Future

videoEditingDetails.description: Transition back to Mark Carney.

Transition to the blue globe animation with digital icons and fast-moving lines. Text '65 billion data points received per year' appears, then changes to 'Reviewing it all would be the equivalent of each supervisor reading the complete works of Shakespeare twice a week, every week of the year.'
Transition to a blurred city skyline with stock market data overlays. Text 'New finance can unlock stronger, more sustainable, and more inclusive growth' appears.
Transition back to Mark Carney.
Transition back to the Sibos logo intro screen.
The text 'Register now on Sibos.com' fades in.
The text '#Sibos' fades in.

climax.description: Mark Carney outlines the Bank of England's approach to innovations like stablecoins: 'with an open mind, but not an open door.'

storylines.description: The Bank of England's approach to the future of finance, focusing on digital innovation, regulatory measures, and SME funding.

content_metadata.title: Future of Finance: A New Bank of England

trimmingSuggestions.description: Consider reducing the length of Scene 2 (0:30-1:07) where long stretches of text overlays on a static screen could be shortened.
Condense Scene 3 (1:07-2:23), summarizing details about access to RTGS and focus on the key message of opening access and promoting competition.
Shorten the initial globe animation in Scene 4 (2:38) to start later, aligning with Mark Carney's mention of data's role in closing SME funding gap.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: It's great to be part of this year's Cybos Conference, which is being hosted in London for
the very first time.
Now London's long been the heart of the global financial system, and it's now also one
of the world's leading FinTech hubs.
And I know you're going to spend most of your time rightly discussing private innovation,
but I want to take this short opportunity to set out the Bank of England's ambitious
plan to support your efforts to create the future of finance.
As this conference recognizes, the world's becoming increasingly digitized and hyper-connected,
and that's bringing enormous new opportunities, and along with it, some challenges.
This new economy requires a new finance.
A new finance to serve the digital economy.
A new finance that balances innovation with resilience.
And that new finance requires a new Bank of England, one which will enable innovation
and empower competition, all well-insuring, the resilience of the financial system.
So let me take a few moments to expand.
First, to enable the digital economy, the very nature of commerce is changing.
Last year, one-fifth of all sales in the UK were online.
Next year, it'll be one quarter.
Use of cash has declined from two-thirds of all payments a decade ago to only one quarter
today.
This new economy is placing new demands on the financial system.
Consumers and businesses increasingly expect transactions to be settled in real time,
and payments across borders to be indistinguishable from those across the street.
And to help private innovation meet these demands, the Bank is leveling the playing field
between old and new.
As you may know, until recently, only commercial banks had direct access to the core of the
payment system, RTGS.
And that made sense in an old world arranged around a series of hubs and spokes, but it's
increasingly an agronistic in the new distributed finance that's emerging.
So now we at the Bank are making it easier for a broader set of firms to plug in and compete
with banks, where the first G20 central bank to do so.
Already, five payment service providers are members of RTGS, and there's a pipeline of
another 20 firms looking to join.
According to demands from innovators, RTGS will now also provide API access to users to
read and write payments data, as well as implementing a system whereby each payment
will be tagged with information in a standardized format across the world, speeding up settlement
and facilitating KYC, AML, and CFT requirements.
The Bank is also using the opportunity of the RTGS rebuild to support more competitive
platform-based finance of SMEs, and in doing so to contribute to closing the biggest
funding gap in this country.
SMEs are the engine room of our economy, but almost half of them don't plan to use external
finance, citing the hassle or the time associated with applying from banks.
Of those that have approached their bank, almost two-fifths have been rejected.
And part of the problem is that the assets the SMEs are seeking to borrow against are
increasingly intangible, such as the value of a brand or a user base, rather than traditional
physical assets like buildings or machinery.
And SMEs that haven't borrowed, of course, lack the track record required for a traditional
credit scoring.
But this shouldn't be the case in a data-rich world.
To close the SME funding gap, SMEs must be able to identify all the data relevant to
their businesses, incorporate it into their individual credit files, and easily share
those files with all potential providers of finance.
And that's why the Bank of England is laying some of the groundwork for a new open platform
for SME lending in the UK.
The platform would turbocharge open banking and empower SMEs, and it would enhance competition
for SME lending, making access to finance quick, easy, and cost-effective.
The Bank of England is also consulting on opening access to our own balance sheet to new
payment providers.
From our perspective, expanding access can improve the transmission of monetary policy,
it can increase competition, and done correctly it can support financial stability.
From the perspective of UK households and businesses, wider access can improve services,
cut costs and speed delivery.
Now the potential for transformation in retail payments is enormous, you know that.
I'll give one example, stablecoins, they seek to offer digital payment via instruments
which retain a reliable value.
If designed and regulated appropriately, stablecoins have the potential to substantially
improve financial inclusion and to dramatically lower the costs of domestic and cross-border
payments.
The Bank of England approaches such innovations as stablecoins and other payment innovations
with an open mind, but not an open door.
Re-recognize that technology is trying to solve problems for consumers, but we want to
make sure that in solving one problem, they don't inadvertently create other more systemic
ones.
And unlike social media, for which standards and regulations are being debated well after
they've been adopted by billions of users, the terms of engagement for such payment innovations
must be adopted in advance of any launch, which is why we want to engage early on with
innovators to help you compete while keeping a system safe.
Systemically important payment systems will have to meet the highest standards of potential
regulation and consumer protection, and they will have to address issues ranging from
any money laundering to data protection to operational resilience.
Using our position at the very heart of the international financial system, Bank of England
is helping to lead the way on these issues through forests such as the G7, the FSB, and
the BIS.
Now let me turn to strengthening the system in the face of new risks.
Today the key competitive advantage in financial services is how firms and their supervisors
collect, store, and analyze the explosion of data.
Using general purpose technologies like the cloud and AI could herald leaner, faster,
and more tailored financial services.
A quarter of major banks' activities and almost one-third of all UK payments' activities
are already hosted on the cloud, and banking is already the second biggest global
spender on AI systems.
These savings can be passed onto customers, and if properly managed, they can improve the
overall resilience of the system.
For these reasons, the Bank of England is very open to greater adoption of the cloud
and usage of AI.
To ensure the benefits of cloud computing are realized, and that the associated risks
are well managed, the banks are going to issue a supervisory statement in the autumn that
sets out our new approach.
The PRA is also exploring how new technologies could streamline firms' compliance and regulatory
processes, while improving our own ability to analyze relevant data.
Let's put it in perspective.
The Bank of England now receives 65 billion data points each year of firm-related information,
reviewing it all would be the equivalent of each supervisor reading the complete works
of Shakespeare twice a week every week of the year.
For firms, while the cloud and AI have reduced the cost of storage and analysis, producing
regulatory submissions is still labor intensive, and the cost to the industry could range between
two and four and a half billion pounds every year.
We see opportunities for much more efficient processes at every stage of supervision.
That includes simplifying our rules, considering models whereby we pull data from firms, and
employing machine learning and AI to analyze the data.
Last month, the bank launched a review on how we host and use regulatory data, and will
embark on proofs of concept with firms to test how we can automatically extract regulatory
data and use AI and ML to analyze it.
This is a rich area for FinTech innovation, and we welcome the chance to work with those
of you who are interested.
Let me conclude.
The new finance has the potential to unlock stronger, more sustainable, and more inclusive
growth.
By taking some of the measures like those that I've outlined today, the Bank of England
can help enable that new economy, empower greater competition, and ensure the resilience
of the financial system at the same time.
But to be as effective as possible, we need and we want to engage with you.
In this conference, you'll be seeing more of us on SyBoss TV, not more of me, thankfully
for you.
Bank of England colleagues will be participating in a number of panels, and we'll be hosting
a number of teachings during the day to give you an opportunity to ask questions about
our plans.
My colleagues and I look forward to speaking with you, to learning from you, and we hope
that you can help us realize these ambitions to improve finance for everyone.
After all, we all remember that finance is not an end to itself.
Finance is a servant of households and entrepreneurs that make this country great, and they are demanding
more sustainable and inclusive and a more prosperous future.
The ultimate test of new finance is whether we can design it and put it into place in a
way that helps deliver just that.
Thank you very much.
Enjoy the conference.

youtube_description: Addressing the major themes at #Sibos 2019, Mark Carney, Governor of the Bank of England (BoE), discusses digitisation, the challenges of balancing #innovation with resilience, and how we can achieve more sustainable and inclusive growth.
youtube_title: Views from the Top: Mark Carney,  Governor of Bank of England (BoE), on Sibos
